 1          Plaintiff Jonathan Itula (“Plaintiff”) brings this Class Action Complaint, on behalf of
 2   himself and all others similarly situated, against Defendant Payactiv, Inc. (“Defendant” or
 3   “Payactiv”), alleging as follows based upon information and belief and investigation of counsel,
 4   except as to the allegations specifically pertaining to Plaintiff, which are based on personal
 5   knowledge:
 6                                       NATURE OF THE CASE
 7          1.      Plaintiff brings this class action against Defendant Payactiv for its failure to
 8   properly secure and safeguard Plaintiff’s and other similarly situated individuals (“Class
 9   Members”) personally identifying information, including names and Social Security numbers
10   (collectively “PII” or “Private Information”). 1
11          2.      Payactiv, Inc. is a financial technology company that provides employers and their
12   employees with earned wage access and related financial wellness services through a digital
13   platform.
14          3.      Plaintiff and Class Members are individuals who were required to indirectly and/or
15   directly provide Defendant with their Private Information. By collecting, storing, and maintaining
16   Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private Information, Payactiv has a resulting duty to secure,
17   maintain, protect, and safeguard the Private Information that it collects and stores against
18   unauthorized access and disclosure through reasonable and adequate data security measures.
19          4.      Despite Payactiv’s duty to safeguard the Private Information of Plaintiff and Class
20   Members, their Private Information in Defendant’s possession was compromised when an
21   unauthorized party gained access to Defendant’s network storage systems and exfiltrated sensitive
22   data stored therein on or about April 3, 2025 (the “Data Breach”). 2

 1          5.      The Data Breach occurred when cybercriminals infiltrated Defendant’s
 2   inadequately protected network servers and accessed highly sensitive PII that was being kept.
 3          6.      After Payactiv discovered the Data Breach on August 19, 2025, it conducted an
 4   investigation which determined that some data may have been acquired on or about April 3, 2025
 5   through August 20, 2025. 3
 6          7.      While Defendant claims to have discovered the breach as early as August 19, 2025,
 7   Defendant did not inform victims of the Data Breach until September 29, 2025. Plaintiff and Class
 8   Members were wholly unaware of the Data Breach until they received letters from Defendant
 9   informing them of it.
10          8.      Indeed, it was not until shortly after September 29, 2025 when Plaintiff received a
11   letter from Defendant notifying him of the Data Breach and theft of his PII.
12          9.      Payactiv maintained the PII of Plaintiff and Class Members in a negligent and/or
13   reckless manner. In particular, the PII was maintained on Payactiv’s computer system and network
14   in a condition vulnerable to cyberattacks. Upon information and belief, the mechanism of the
15   cyberattack and potential for improper disclosure of Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII was a
16   known risk to Defendant, and thus Defendant was on notice that failing to take steps necessary to
17   secure the PII from those risks left that property in a dangerous condition.
18          10.     Defendant disregarded the rights of Plaintiff and Class Members by intentionally,
19   willfully, recklessly, and/or negligently failing to implement adequate and reasonable measures to
20   ensure that Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII was safeguarded, failing to take available steps to
21   prevent unauthorized disclosure of data and failing to follow applicable, required and appropriate
22   protocols, policies, and procedures regarding the encryption of data, even for internal use.
23          11.     As a result, Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII was compromised by an
24   unauthorized third-party. Plaintiff and Class Members have a continuing interest in ensuring that
25   their information is and remains safe and are entitled to injunctive and other equitable relief.

 1          12.     As a direct and proximate result of Defendant’s failure to implement and follow
 2   basic security procedures, Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private Information is now in the hands

 4          13.     Plaintiff and Class Members are now at a significantly increased and certainly

 7   devote substantially more time, money, and energy to protect themselves, to the extent possible,
 8   from these crimes.
 9          14.     Plaintiff, on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated, alleges claims for
10   negligence, breach of implied contract, unjust enrichment and declaratory judgment arising from
11   the Data Breach. Plaintiff seeks damages and injunctive relief, including the adoption reasonably
12   sufficient practices to safeguard the Private Information in Defendant’s custody to prevent
13   incidents like the Data Breach from reoccurring in the future, and for Defendant to provide identity
14   theft protective services to Plaintiff and Class Members for their lifetimes.

 1          24.     Pursuant to their relationship with Defendant’s services, Plaintiff and Class
 2   Members directly or indirectly entrusted Payactiv with their sensitive Private Information.
 3          25.     Plaintiff and Class Members value the confidentiality of their Private Information
 4   and, accordingly, have taken reasonable steps to maintain the confidentiality of their Private
 5   Information.
 6          26.     In entrusting their Private Information to Defendant, Plaintiff and Class Members
 7   reasonably expected that Defendant would safeguard their highly sensitive information.
 8          27.     By obtaining, collecting, and storing Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private
 9   Information, Payactiv assumed equitable and legal duties to safeguard Plaintiff’s and Class
10   Members’ highly sensitive information, to only use this information for business purposes, and to
11   only make authorized disclosures.
12          28.     Despite these duties, Payactiv failed to implement reasonable data security
13   measures to protect Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private Information and ultimately allowed
14   threat actors to breach its computer systems and exfiltrate Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private
15   Information stored therein.
16   THE VALUE OF PRIVATE INFORMATION AND EFFECTS OF UNAUTHORIZED DISCLOSURE
17          29.     Payactiv understood that the Private Information it collects was highly sensitive
18   and of significant value to those who would use it for wrongful purposes.
19          30.     Payactiv also knew that a breach of its computer systems, and exposure of the
20   Private Information stored therein, would result in the increased risk of identity theft and fraud
21   against the individuals whose Private Information was compromised.
22          31.     These risks are not theoretical; in recent years, numerous high-profile breaches
23   have occurred at business such as Equifax, Facebook, Yahoo, Marriott, Anthem, and many others.
24          32.     Private Information has considerable value and constitutes an enticing and well-
25   known target to hackers. Hackers can easily sell stolen data as there has been “proliferation of

 3          33.     As the FTC recognizes, identity thieves can use this information to commit an array
 4   of crimes including identity theft, and medical and financial fraud. 6 The prevalence of data
 5   breaches and identity theft has increased dramatically in recent years, accompanied by a parallel
 6   and growing economic drain on individual, businesses, and government entities in the U.S. In 2023
 7   alone, there were 6,077 recorded breaches exposing more than 17 billion records - representing a

10   2017 to 5.7 million in 2021. 8

12   next two years from “social engineering and ransomware” as nation-states and cybercriminals

17   data compromises in the U.S. in a single year since such instances began being tracked in 2005. 10

 1          36.     The ramifications of Payactiv’s failure to keep Plaintiff’s and Class Members’
 2   Private Information secure are long-lasting and severe. Once Private Information is stolen,
 3   fraudulent use of that information and damage to victims may continue for years. According to the
 4   U.S. Government Accountability Office, which conducted a study regarding data breaches: “[I]n
 5   some cases, stolen data may be held for up to a year or more before being used to commit identity
 6   theft. Further, once stolen data has been sold or posted on the [Dark] Web, fraudulent use of that
 7   information may continue for years. As a result, studies that attempt to measure the harm resulting
 8   from data breaches cannot necessarily rule out all future harm.” 11
 9          37.     Even if stolen Private Information does not include financial or payment card
10   account information, that does not mean there has been no harm, or that the breach does not cause
11   a substantial risk of identity theft. Freshly stolen information can be used with success against
12   victims in specifically targeted efforts to commit identity theft known as social engineering or
13   spear phishing. In these forms of attack, the criminal uses the previously obtained PII about the
14   individual, such as name, address, email address, and affiliations, to gain trust and increase the
15   likelihood that a victim will be deceived into providing the criminal with additional information.
16          38.     The specific types of personal data compromised in the Data Breach makes the
17   information particularly valuable to thieves and leaves Plaintiff and other Class Members
18   especially vulnerable to identity theft, tax fraud, medical fraud, credit and bank fraud, and more.
19          39.     Social Security Numbers—Unlike credit or debit card numbers in a payment card
20   data breach—which can quickly be frozen and reissued in the aftermath of a breach—unique Social
21   Security Numbers cannot be easily replaced. Even when such numbers are replaced, the process
22   of doing so results in a major inconvenience to the subject person, requiring a wholesale review of
23   the person’s relationships with government agencies and any number of private companies in order
24   to update the person’s accounts with those entities.

 1           40.    Indeed, the Social Security Administration warns that the process of replacing a
 2   Social Security Number is a difficult one that creates other types of problems, and that it will not
 3   be a complete remedy for the affected person:
 4
                    Keep in mind that a new number probably will not solve all your
 5                  problems. This is because other governmental agencies (such as the
                    IRS and state motor vehicle agencies) and private businesses (such
 6                  as banks and credit reporting companies) likely will have records
                    under your old number. Along with other personal information,
 7                  credit reporting companies use the number to identify your credit
                    record. So using a new number will not guarantee you a fresh start.
 8
                    This is especially true if your other personal information, such as
 9                  your name and address, remains the same.

10                  If you receive a new Social Security Number, you should not be able
                    to use the old number anymore.
11

12                  For some victims of identity theft, a new number actually creates
                    new problems. If the old credit information is not associated with
13                  your new number, the absence of any credit history under the new
                    number may make more difficult for you to get credit. 12

15           41.    Social Security numbers allow individuals to apply for credit cards, student loans,
16   mortgages, and other lines of credit - among other services. Often social security numbers can be
17   used to obtain medical goods or services, including prescriptions. They are also used to apply for
18   a host of government benefits. Access to such a wide range of assets makes Social Security
19   numbers a prime target for cybercriminals and a particularly attractive form of PII to steal and then
20   sell.
21           42.    Based on the value of Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII to cybercriminals,
22   Payactiv knew or should have known the importance of safeguarding the PII entrusted to it and of
23   the foreseeable consequences if its data security systems were breached. Payactiv failed, however,
24   to take adequate cyber security measures to prevent the Data Breach from occurring.

     PAYACTIV BREACHED ITS DUTY TO PROTECT PLAINTIFF’S AND CLASS MEMBERS’ PRIVATE

 3             43.    On or about August 19, 2025, Payactiv became aware of a cybersecurity event

 4   impacting its network storage systems. Following the discovery of the incident, Defendant began

 5   an investigation to discover the scope of the suspicious activity.

 6             44.    Defendant’s investigation confirmed that on or about April 3, 2025, an

 7   unauthorized third-party had gained access to defendant’s network and successfully exfiltrated

 8   Private Information stored therein. The Private Information exfiltrated in the Data Breach includes

 9   individuals, names and Social Security Numbers.

10             45.    On or around October 14, 2025, nearly six months after the Data Breach began,

11   Payactiv reported the Data Breach to the Office of the Texas Attorney General, indicating the Data

12   Breach compromised the Private Information of 10,973 Texas residents. 13

13             46.    Although the breach began in April 2025, PayActiv did not begin notifying affected

14   individuals whose PII Defendant confirmed was potentially compromised because of the Data

15   Breach until on or around September 29, 2025. The Notice provided basic details of the Data

16   Breach and Defendant’s recommended next steps.

17             47.    The Notice included, inter alia, an explanation that Defendant had learned on

18   August 19, 2025 that a third party viewed files in its system and on September 12, 2025 had taken

19   steps to respond. But the Notice lacked sufficient information on how the breach occurred, what

20   safeguards have been taken since then to safeguard further attacks, and/or where the information

21   hacked exists today.

22             48.    Based on Defendant’s announcement of the Data Breach, the cyberattack was

23   expressly designed to gain access to private and confidential data of specific individuals, including

24   (among other things) the PII of Plaintiff and the Class Members and that the cybercriminals were

25   successful in exfiltrating sensitive information from Defendant’s network.

 1          49.     All in all, the Private Information of thousands of individuals was compromised in
 2   the Data Breach.
 3          50.     The Data Breach occurred as a direct result of Payactiv’s failure to implement and
 4   follow basic security procedures to protect its current and former customers’ Private Information
 5   that it had collected and stored.
 6   PAYACTIV FAILED TO COMPLY WITH FTC GUIDELINES
 7          51.     Payactiv is prohibited by the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45 (“FTC
 8   Act”) from engaging in “unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.” The
 9   Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) has concluded that a company’s failure to maintain reasonable
10   and appropriate data security for consumers’ sensitive personal information is an “unfair practice”
11   in violation of the FTC Act.
12          52.     The FTC has promulgated numerous guides for businesses that highlight the
13   importance of implementing reasonable data security practices. According to the FTC, the need
14   for data security should be factored into all business decision-making. 14
15          53.     Among other guidance, the FTC recommends the following cybersecurity
16   guidelines for businesses in order to protect sensitive information in their systems: 15
17                  a.    Identify all connections to the computers where sensitive information is
18                        stored;

19                  b.    Assess the vulnerability of each connection to commonly known or
                          reasonably foreseeable attacks;
20
                    c.    Do not store sensitive consumer data on any computer with an internet
21                        connection unless it is essential for conducting their business;
22
                    d.    Scan computers on their network to identify and profile the operating system
23                        and open network services. If services are not needed, they should be disabled
                          to prevent hacks or other potential security problems. For example, if email

 1   unfair act or practice prohibited by Section 5 of the FTC Act. Orders resulting from these actions

 3           56.     Payactiv failed to properly implement basic data security practices. Payactiv’s
 4   failure to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect against unauthorized access to
 5   its customers’ PII constitutes an unfair act of practice prohibited by Section 5 of the FTC Act.
 6           57.     Payactiv was at all times fully aware of its obligations to protect the PII of its
 7   customers given the reams of PII that it had access to as Plaintiff and the Class Members’ financial

10   PAYACTIV’S FAILURE TO PREVENT, IDENTIFY, AND TIMELY REPORT THE DATA BREACH
11           58.     Payactiv admits that an unauthorized third-party accessed its information
12   technology system and that Defendant discovered this unauthorized access on or about August 19,
13   2025.
14           59.     Payactiv failed to take necessary precautions and failed to employ adequate
15   measures necessary to protect its computer systems against unauthorized access and keep
16   Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ Private Information secure.
17           60.     The Private Information that Payactiv allowed to be exposed in the Data Breach is
18   the type of private information that Payactiv knew or should have known would be the target of
19   cyberattacks.
20           61.     Despite its own knowledge of the inherent risks of cyberattacks, and

22   its systems and security practices were inadequate to reasonably safeguard individuals’ Private
23   Information.

 1          62.     The FTC directs businesses to use an intrusion detection system to expose a breach
 2   as soon as it occurs, monitor activity for attempted hacks, and have an immediate response plan if
 3   a breach occurs. 18 Immediate notification to individuals impacted by a data breach is critical so
